questions.text: (a) From which end of the ovule, and how does the pollen tube gain its entry into the embryo sac of a Hibiscus flower ? (b) State the fate of the male nuclei present in the pollen tube.

answer.text:
(a) The pollen tube enters the ovule from the micropylar end and passes into a synergid, guided by the filiform apparatus.
(b) Double fertilisation: one male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the primary endosperm nucleus (triple fusion); the other male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote (syngamy).

questions.text: Study the diagram given below showing the modes of pollination. Answer the questions that follow. (i) The given diagram shows three methods of pollen transfer in plants. What are the technical terms used for pollen transfer methods '1', '2' and '3' ? (ii) How do the following plants achieve pollination successfully ? (1) Water lily (2) Vallisneria (iii) Flowering plants have developed many devices to avoid inbreeding depression. Explain one hereditary and one physiological device which helps plants to achieve this target.

answer.text:
(i) (1) Autogamy; (2) Geitonogamy; (3) Xenogamy.
(ii) (1) Water lily — pollinated by insects or wind.
(2) Vallisneria — the female flowers reach the water surface on long stalks; the male flowers or pollen are released onto the water and carried by the water current to the female flowers to achieve pollination.
(iii) Genetic (self-incompatibility): prevents the self-pollen of the same flower or plant from fertilising the ovules, by inhibiting pollen germination and pollen-tube growth in the pistil.
Physiological: pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised — either the pollen matures earlier and the stigma later, or the pollen matures later than the stigma.

questions.text: One of the major approaches of crop improvement programme is Artificial Hybridisation. Explain the steps involved in making sure that only the desired pollen grain pollinate the stigma of a bisexual flower by a plant breeder.

answer.text:
Steps in artificial hybridisation:
• Emasculation — removal of the anthers from the flower bud before the anther dehisces.
• Bagging — covering the emasculated flower with a bag of suitable size to prevent contamination of its stigma with unwanted pollen.
• Dusting the desired pollen on the stigma and re-bagging.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain the monosporic development of embryo sac in the ovule of an angiosperm. (ii) Draw a diagram of the mature embryo sac of an angiospermic ovule and label any four parts in it.

answer.text:
Megasporogenesis and the development of the embryo sac:
The megaspore mother cell (2n) undergoes meiosis to form a tetrad of four megaspores (n). Three of these degenerate, leaving one functional megaspore. This functional megaspore undergoes three successive mitotic divisions without cell-wall formation (free-nuclear division) to give an 8-nucleate stage. Cell walls then form, organising it into the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac shown below (with three antipodals at the chalazal end, two synergids and one egg at the micropylar end, and a central cell with two polar nuclei).

questions.text: (a) Explain how it is ensured that the orchid Ophrys is pollinated by a specific species of bee. (b) Describe co-evolution with the help of this example.

answer.text:
(a) The orchid $Ophrys$ employs 'sexual deceit' to get pollinated by a species of bee: one petal of the flower resembles the female of the bee in size, colour and markings; the male bee is attracted and pseudocopulates with the flower, getting dusted with pollen; when the same bee pseudocopulates with another flower, it transfers the pollen to it.
(b) If the pattern of the female bee changes during evolution, the flower must co-evolve to keep resembling the female bee, otherwise it will not get pollinated.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain the process of double fertilization in an angiosperm starting from the germination of pollen grains on the stigma, mentioning the ploidy of the end products formed at the end. State the role of synergids during the course of the process. (ii) Why does the development of endosperm precede that of the embryo ?

answer.text: The pollen tube passes down the style, and the generative cell divides mitotically into two male gametes, which are discharged into the embryo sac through the micropyle (the filiform apparatus of the synergids guides the entry of the pollen tube at the micropylar end). One male gamete fuses with the egg to form the diploid (2n) zygote (syngamy); the other male nucleus (n) fuses with the secondary nucleus (2n) to form the triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus (triple fusion). Because two fusions occur within one embryo sac, this is called double fertilisation. (ii) The endosperm provides assured nutrition to the developing embryo.

questions.text: (A) (i) Describe the process of megasporogenesis in an angiosperm. (ii) Draw a diagram of a mature embryo sac of an angiosperm. Label its any four parts.

answer.text:
(i) Development of the female gametophyte (embryo sac): the megaspore mother cell (2n) undergoes meiosis to form a tetrad of four megaspores (n); three degenerate and one functional megaspore remains. This megaspore undergoes three free-nuclear mitotic divisions (without cell-wall formation) to reach the 8-nucleate stage, after which cell walls are laid down to form the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac.
(ii) A typical embryo sac (diagram below) is 7-celled and 8-nucleate: at the chalazal end are three antipodal cells; in the centre is the large central cell with two polar nuclei; and at the micropylar end is the egg apparatus (one egg cell and two synergids).

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain how does double fertilisation take place in a flowering plant. (ii) Write the fate of the products of double fertilization in these plants.

answer.text:
(i) After entering one of the synergids, the pollen tube releases its two male gametes into the cytoplasm of the synergid. One male gamete moves towards the egg cell and fuses with its nucleus, completing syngamy to form the diploid zygote. The other male gamete moves towards the two polar nuclei in the central cell and fuses with them (triple fusion) to form the triploid Primary Endosperm Nucleus (PEN) / Primary Endosperm Cell (PEC). This is double fertilisation.
(ii) The Primary Endosperm Cell (PEC) develops into the endosperm, while the zygote develops into the embryo.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain the structure of a typical monocotyledonous embryo of a flowering plant. (ii) How are multiple embryos formed in a citrus fruit ? What is the mechanism known as ?

answer.text:
(i) The embryo of a monocotyledonous seed (diagram below) has a single cotyledon called the scutellum, situated laterally (towards one side) of the embryonal axis. At the lower end of the embryonal axis are the radicle and the root cap, enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath called the coleorhiza. The portion of the embryonal axis above the level of attachment of the scutellum is the epicotyl, which has a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure called the coleoptile.
(ii) Some of the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos; this phenomenon (of forming embryos without fertilisation, giving many embryos) is apomixis / polyembryony.

questions.text: (a) How is the interaction between Ophrys and its specific bee pollinator one of the best examples of co-evolution ? Explain.

answer.text: One petal of $Ophrys$ bears an uncanny resemblance to the female of a particular bee species in size, colour and markings. The male bee is attracted to what it perceives as a female and pseudo-copulates with the flower; during this process it is dusted with pollen from the flower, and when it pseudo-copulates with another flower it transfers the pollen — bringing about pollination.

questions.text: Flowering plants with hermaphrodite flowers have developed many reproductive strategies to ensure cross-pollination. Study the given outbreeding devices adopted by certain flowering plants (all plants belong to the same species; '×' = no pollen tube growth/inhibition of pollen germination on stigma, '✓' = pollen germination on stigma) and answer the questions that follow. (a) Name and define the outbreeding device described in the above table. (b) Explain what would have been the disadvantage to the plant in the absence of the given strategy.

answer.text:
(a) Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or another flower of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or the growth of the pollen tube in the pistil (it is also brought about by the non-synchronisation of pollen release and stigma receptivity — either the pollen is released before the stigma becomes receptive, or the stigma becomes receptive well before the release of the pollen).
(b) It would have led to inbreeding depression.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain the structure of a mature embryo sac of a typical flowering plant. (ii) How is triple fusion achieved in these plants ?

answer.text:
(i) Structure of a typical angiosperm embryo sac (diagram below): three cells grouped together at the micropylar end constitute the egg apparatus, which consists of two synergids and one egg cell; the synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called the filiform apparatus. Three cells are at the chalazal end and are called the antipodals. The large central cell has two polar nuclei. Thus, a typical embryo sac at maturity, though 8-nucleate, is 7-celled.
(ii) During double fertilisation, one of the two male gametes fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell (triple fusion) to produce the triploid Primary Endosperm Nucleus (PEN).

(c)(i) Advantage of autogamy — an assured seed set with no dependence on pollinators, so that a pure breed can be obtained. Disadvantage — no genetic variation (it leads to inbreeding depression).

questions.text: (a) (i) How does a farmer use dormancy of seed to his advantage ? (ii) Differentiate between pea seed and castor seed.

answer.text:
(a)(i) Seed dormancy is crucial for the storage (dehydration) of seeds, so that they can be used to raise the crops in the next season, be used as a source of food, or be used for commercial purposes.
(ii) Difference between a pea seed and a castor seed (any one): a pea seed is a non-endospermic (non-albuminous) seed — no endosperm is left in it as it is fully consumed during embryo development; a castor seed is an endospermic (albuminous) seed — it contains some endosperm, as it is not completely consumed during embryo development.

questions.text: (a) Do all pollen grains remain viable for the same length of time ? Support your answer with two suitable examples. (b) How are pollen grains stored in pollen banks ?

answer.text:
(a) No. The viability of pollen grains after their release varies with the species: in cereals such as rice and wheat, the pollen grains lose viability within about 30 minutes of their release, whereas in some members of the Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae, they maintain viability for months.
(b) Pollen grains can be stored for years using cryopreservation techniques — in liquid nitrogen at $-196\,^{\circ}$C (this makes it possible to build pollen banks).

questions.text: Answer the following questions : (a) Explain the different ways by which apomictic seeds can be developed. (b) Mention one advantage of apomictic seeds for farmers.

answer.text:
(a) Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction (seeds are produced without fertilisation). It occurs in two main ways: in some species (of the Asteraceae and grasses) the diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation; and in some species the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.
(b) Importance: in apomictic seeds there is no segregation of the hybrid characters in the progeny, so farmers can go on using the hybrid seeds to raise a new crop year after year; if hybrid seeds are made apomictic, the farmer need not buy fresh hybrid seeds every year, so it is cost-effective.

questions.text: List any three outbreeding devices that flowering plants have developed for cross-pollination and explain how they help to encourage cross-pollination.

answer.text:
Outbreeding devices that prevent self-pollination (any three):
– Self-incompatibility: a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollination by inhibiting the germination of pollen (from the same flower, or a different flower of the same plant) on the stigma.
– Unisexual flowers have no chance of self-pollination.
– Receptivity of male and female parts: pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised.
– Position of male and female parts: the anther and the stigma are placed at different positions so that the pollen cannot come into contact with the stigma of the same flower.
– Unisexual plants (male and female flowers on different plants) have no chance of self-pollination.

questions.text: (i) Double fertilisation is an event unique to all flowering plants. Explain the process. (ii) Give a reason for the following : (1) A seed of an orange has many embryos. (2) Cashew is a false fruit but Guava is a true fruit.

answer.text:
(i) Double fertilisation is the occurrence of two types of fusion — syngamy and triple fusion — within the embryo sac of an angiosperm.
• Syngamy: fusion of one male gamete with the egg cell, forming the (diploid) zygote.
• Triple fusion: fusion of the other male gamete with the two polar nuclei, producing the (triploid) primary endosperm nucleus.
(ii)(1) In apomixis, some of the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing and protrude into the embryo sac to form embryos.
(2) In cashew, the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation along with the ovary (a false fruit develops from a part other than the ovary), whereas guava fruit develops only from the ovary after fertilisation.

questions.text: (b) Name any two outbreeding devices that flowering plants have developed and explain how they help in encouraging cross-pollination.

answer.text:
Devices/mechanisms that prevent self-pollination (any two, with explanation):
• Unisexuality — the production of unisexual flowers prevents self-pollination.
• Non-synchrony — the release of pollen and the receptivity of the stigma are not synchronised (pollen is released before the stigma is receptive, or the stigma becomes receptive well before the pollen is released).
• Different positions — the anther and stigma are placed at different positions, so the pollen cannot come into contact with the stigma.
• Self-incompatibility — a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising the ovule by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen-tube growth in the pistil.

questions.text: Observe the diagram given below showing the menstrual cycle of a normal human female and answer the questions that follow (numbers indicate the days of the menstrual cycle) : (i) What are the suitable technical terms used for the following ? (1) Days 1–7 (2) Days 8–12 (3) Days 16–28 (4) Days 13–15 (ii) Explain the role of ovarian and pituitary hormones during the following time periods : (1) Days 8–12 (2) Days 13–15 (3) Days 16–28

answer.text:
(i) (1) Menstrual phase; (2) Follicular / proliferative phase; (3) Luteal / secretory phase; (4) Ovulatory phase.
(ii) During the follicular phase, FSH from the pituitary stimulates follicular development and the secretion of estrogen by the growing follicle; a mid-cycle surge of LH triggers ovulation; in the luteal phase the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which maintains the endometrium in readiness for implantation.

questions.text: (b) (i) Draw a diagrammatic sectional view of ovary of human female and label the following : (1) Blood vessels (2) Primary follicle (3) Tertiary follicle (4) Ovum. (ii) At which stage of life are primary follicles formed in a human female ? (iii) Explain the events (both hormonal and structural) that occur at the time of ovulation till the onset of the next menstrual cycle.

answer.text:
T.S. of the mammalian ovary (labelled below) shows follicles at various stages of development — the primary follicle, the tertiary follicle showing the antrum, the ovum, and the blood vessels — set in the stroma. (ii) The ovum is at the embryonic (secondary-oocyte) stage at ovulation.
(iii) Both LH and FSH reach peak levels in the middle of the menstrual cycle; the rapid rise of LH to a maximum (the LH surge) induces the rupture of the Graafian follicle and causes ovulation. The ovulatory phase is followed by the luteal phase, during which the remaining parts of the Graafian follicle transform into the corpus luteum, which secretes a large amount of progesterone to maintain the endometrium. In the absence of fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates, causing the endometrium to disintegrate, which leads to menstruation.

questions.text: (b) (i) Mention the site where fertilisation of the ovum occurs in a human female. Explain the process of fertilization and mention how polyspermy is prevented. (ii) Name the embryonic stage that gets implanted in the uterus. Explain the process of implantation in a human female.

answer.text:
(i) Fertilisation takes place at the ampullary-isthmic junction (the ampulla) of the fallopian tube. A sperm comes into contact with the zona pellucida of the ovum; the secretion of the acrosome helps the sperm enter the cytoplasm of the ovum, which induces the completion of meiosis II to form the haploid ovum (ootid). The haploid nuclei of the sperm and the ovum then fuse to form the diploid zygote. Contact of the sperm with the zona pellucida induces changes in the membrane that block the entry of additional sperms.
(ii) Blastocyst — the trophoblast layer of the blastocyst attaches to the endometrium; the inner cell mass differentiates into the embryo; the uterine cells divide rapidly and the blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium (implantation).

rows: The endometrium regenerates through proliferation under the influence of estrogen.

questions.text: (B) Given below is the diagram of human ovum surrounded by a few sperms. Observe the diagram and answer the questions that follows : (i) Compare the fate of sperms 'P', 'Q' and 'R' shown in the diagram. (ii) Write the role of Zona pellucida in this process. (iii) Analyse the changes occurring in the ovum after the entry of sperm. (iv) How acrosome and middle piece of a human sperm are able to play an important role in human fertilization ?

answer.text:
(i) P is able to penetrate / fertilise the ovum, whereas Q and R are unable to penetrate / fertilise it.
(ii) When a sperm comes into contact with the zona pellucida layer of the ovum, it induces changes in the membrane that block the entry of any additional sperms.
(iii) The entry of the sperm induces the completion of the meiotic division of the secondary oocyte, forming the second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid).
(iv) Acrosome — it is filled with enzymes that help the sperm enter the cytoplasm of the ovum. Middle piece — it has numerous mitochondria which produce the energy for the movement of the tail, facilitating sperm motility for fertilisation.

questions.text: (B) The reproductive cycle in the female primates is called menstrual cycle. The first menstruation begins at puberty. Answer the following questions : (i) Name the four phases of menstrual cycle in a proper sequence. (ii) How long does the menstrual phase last in a menstrual cycle ? (iii) When and why hormones estrogen and progesterone reach their peak levels respectively, in the menstrual cycle ? (iv) Give the significance of LH surge.

answer.text:
(i) The correct sequence of the phases of the menstrual cycle: menstrual phase $\rightarrow$ proliferative / follicular phase $\rightarrow$ ovulatory phase $\rightarrow$ luteal / secretory phase.
(ii) The menstrual (bleeding) phase lasts about 3–5 days.
(iii) Estrogen reaches its peak during the proliferative phase, just before ovulation, because it is secreted by the growing follicles; progesterone reaches its peak during the luteal (secretory) phase, because it is secreted by the corpus luteum.
(iv) The LH surge induces the rupture of the Graafian follicle / the release of the ovum (ovulation).

questions.text: (b) (i) Explain the structure of testicular lobules in human male reproductive system. Name the two types of cells present in the seminiferous tubules and state their role. (ii) Describe the role of hypothalamic hormone GnRH in spermatogenesis.

answer.text:
(i) Each testicular lobule consists of 1–3 highly coiled seminiferous tubules in which the sperms are produced. The seminiferous tubules contain two types of cells: the male germ cells (spermatogonia), which undergo meiotic divisions finally leading to sperm formation; and the Sertoli cells, which provide nutrition to the germ cells.
(ii) GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary gland and stimulates the secretion of the two gonadotropins — luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).

questions.text: (b) (i) Name and explain the structural organisation of the male sex accessory ducts in the human male reproductive system. (ii) Describe the role of gonadotropin FSH in the regulation of spermatogenesis.

answer.text:
(i) The path of the sperm from the testis: the seminiferous tubules of the testis open into the vasa efferentia through the rete testis; the vasa efferentia leave the testis and open into the epididymis, located along the posterior surface of each testis; the epididymis leads to the vas deferens, which ascends into the abdomen and loops over the urinary bladder.
(ii) FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and stimulates the secretion of certain factors that help in the process of spermiogenesis (a part of spermatogenesis).

questions.text: (b) (i) Explain menstrual phase in the menstrual cycle of human female. (ii) Why is follicular phase also called proliferative phase ? (iii) Explain the events that occur in Graafian follicle at the time of ovulation and thereafter. (iv) Draw a Graafian follicle and label – Antrum and secondary oocyte.

(i) Menstrual phase: the endometrial lining of the uterus, along with its blood vessels, breaks down and is discharged as the menstrual flow through the vagina; the flow lasts about 3–5 days.

(ii) The follicular phase is also called the proliferative phase because during it the endometrium regenerates by the proliferation of its cells.

(iii) At ovulation the Graafian follicle ruptures and releases the secondary oocyte; the remaining part of the Graafian follicle is transformed into the corpus luteum.

questions.text: (a) Trace the events from fertilization till implantation of blastocyst in human female. Also mention the site where fertilization takes place.

answer.text: (a) After the entry of the sperm into the female gamete, the secondary oocyte completes meiotic division II to produce a haploid ovum (ootid); the nucleus of the sperm and that of the ootid then fuse to form the diploid zygote. The zygote moves through the isthmus of the oviduct towards the uterus and undergoes mitotic cleavage to form blastomeres. The embryo with 8–16 blastomeres is called the morula, which divides further and transforms into the blastocyst. The blastocyst has an outer layer (trophoblast) and an inner cell mass; the trophoblast becomes attached to the endometrium, the uterine wall grows over the blastocyst, and it becomes embedded in the endometrium — this is implantation. The site of fertilisation is the ampullary region (the ampullary–isthmic junction) of the fallopian tube.

questions.text: (a) Oogenesis is a discontinuous process that begins before birth and is completed after puberty. (i) Trace the development of a gamete mother cell till its release from the ovary during ovulation. (ii) Name the two pituitary hormones that play an important role in the process.

answer.text:
(a)(i) Oogenesis (diagram below): the oogonia (2n gamete mother cells) multiply by mitosis in the foetal ovary and differentiate into primary oocytes; each primary oocyte gets surrounded by follicle cells to form a primary follicle. The primary oocyte remains arrested in prophase-I until puberty; after puberty, the oocyte inside the tertiary follicle completes meiosis-I to form a haploid secondary oocyte and a first polar body. The tertiary follicle changes into the Graafian follicle. The secondary oocyte starts meiosis-II and then stops; the Graafian follicle ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (the ovum) from the ovary (ovulation).
(ii) The hormones that increase during the follicular phase are luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).

– Estrogen: responsible for the maturation of the primary follicle into the Graafian follicle and for the regeneration of the endometrial lining.

questions.text: (a) Briefly explain the events of fertilisation and implantation in an adult human female.

answer.text:
(a)
– Fertilisation: fertilisation occurs in the ampulla (the ampullary-isthmic junction) of the fallopian tube. When a sperm comes in contact with the ovum, it induces changes in the zona pellucida that block the entry of additional sperms, ensuring that only one sperm fertilises the ovum. Secretions of the acrosome help the sperm to enter the cytoplasm of the ovum by dissolving the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane. The entry of the sperm induces the completion of meiosis-II of the secondary oocyte; the nucleus of the ovum (ootid) then fuses with that of the sperm to form a diploid zygote.
– Implantation: the trophoblast layer of the blastocyst gets attached to the endometrium; the uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst, so that the blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium of the uterus.

(a) Comparison of two contraceptive methods:
• Oral pills — Merits: effective with fewer side-effects, reversible, cost-effective and user-friendly. Demerits: may have side-effects when taken for a long time; if not taken in the correct pattern they may fail to prevent conception.

questions.text: (a) Stability, as one of the properties of genetic material, was very evident in one of the very early experiments in genetics. Name the scientist and describe his experiment. State the conclusion he arrived at.

answer.text:
Griffith's transformation experiment: Frederick Griffith took two strains of $Streptococcus\ pneumoniae$ — the R strain (rough, non-virulent) and the S strain (smooth, virulent, with a mucous coat) — and injected them into mice.
• S strain → the mice die.
• R strain → the mice live.
• Heat-killed S strain → the mice live.
• Heat-killed S strain + live R strain → the mice die.
Conclusion: the R-strain bacteria were transformed by the heat-killed S strain. A 'transforming principle' transferred from the heat-killed S strain enabled the R strain to synthesise the smooth polysaccharide coat — this must be due to the transfer of genetic material. The heat that killed the bacteria did not destroy some properties of the genetic material, which shows its stability.

(i) Cross between two carriers, $Hb^A Hb^S \times Hb^A Hb^S$ (Punnett square below), gives offspring in the ratio 2 : 1 : 1 (carrier : disease-free : diseased). In sickle-cell anaemia, adenine is substituted by thymine (at the sixth codon of the $\beta$-globin gene).
(ii) The inheritance of flower colour in the garden pea plant follows the Law of Dominance, because violet colour is dominant over white colour: $WW$ (violet) $\times ww$ (white) gives all violet ($Ww$) F$_1$ progeny. In snapdragon, the flower colour shows incomplete dominance and all the F$_1$ progeny are pink, because red colour is not completely dominant over the recessive white colour: $RR$ (red) $\times rr$ (white) gives all pink ($Rr$) F$_1$ progeny.

questions.text: What did Henking observe in his experiments on insects that led to the discovery of sex chromosome ? How did his observation contribute to our understanding of sex determination ?

answer.text: Henking traced a specific nuclear structure (the X-body) all through spermatogenesis in a few insects, and observed that 50 % of the sperm received this special structure after spermatogenesis whereas the other 50 % did not. This observation later helped in understanding sex determination: the eggs fertilised by a sperm carrying the X chromosome developed into females, while the eggs fertilised by a sperm without the X chromosome developed into males.

questions.text: (a) Describe the experiment conducted by T.H. Morgan on Drosophila melanogaster involving eye colour and body colour. (b) How did the results deviate from Mendelian inheritance pattern ? (c) Explain the two genetic terms used by Morgan for his observations.

answer.text:
(a) In his linkage experiment, Morgan hybridised yellow-bodied, white-eyed females with brown-bodied, red-eyed males and then intercrossed their F$_1$ progeny.
(b) He observed that the two genes did not segregate independently of each other (as expected in the Mendelian pattern); the ratio deviated from the 9:3:3:1 ratio expected when the genes segregate independently.
(c) The terms he coined: Linkage — to describe the physical association of two genes present on the same chromosome; and Recombination — the generation of non-parental gene combinations.

questions.text: (b) (i) How does a chromosomal disorder differ from a Mendelian disorder ? Write one example for each. questions.text: A homozygous tall pea plant with green seeds is crossed with a homozygous dwarf pea plant with yellow seeds. (i) Write the possible phenotype and genotype of F$_1$ generation. answer.text:
(i) Phenotype — tall plant with yellow seeds; genotype — $TtYy$.
(ii) Law of Dominance: of two contrasting traits, only one (the dominant) appears in the $F_1$ generation, while the other (recessive) remains unexpressed.
Law of Segregation: the alleles of a pair remain together in the hybrid and segregate at the time of gamete formation.

questions.text: (b) It is sometimes observed that the F$_1$ progeny has a phenotype that does not resemble either of the two parents and has intermediate phenotype. Explain by taking a suitable example and working out the cross upto F$_2$ progeny.

Incomplete dominance in the snapdragon (dog flower, $Antirrhinum$):
Red $RR$ × white $rr$ gives $Rr$, which is pink (a blend). On selfing ($Rr \times Rr$), the $F_2$ (below) shows a phenotypic ratio of 1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White and a genotypic ratio of $RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1$.

questions.text: (b) (i) Why is sickle-cell anaemia, a human blood disorder so named ? (ii) Explain the genetic basis that results in the expression of this disorder. (iii) Work out a cross to explain how normal parents may have a sickle-cell anaemic child.

answer.text:
(i) The red blood cell in such patients takes up a sickle shape instead of the normal biconcave shape.
(ii) The defect is caused by the substitution of glutamic acid (Glu) by valine (Val) at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain of haemoglobin; this results from a single base substitution at the sixth codon of the beta-globin gene, from GAG to GUG.
(iii) A cross of two carriers ($Hb^A Hb^S \times Hb^A Hb^S$) gives the offspring shown below — it is an autosomal recessive disorder.

questions.text: (b) Differentiate between the following : (i) Polygenic Inheritance and Pleiotropy (ii) Dominance, Codominance and Incomplete dominance.

answer.text:
(i) Polygenic inheritance — the inheritance of a trait that is controlled by three or more genes, where the phenotype reflects the additive contribution of all the alleles. Pleiotropy — when a single gene shows multiple phenotypic expressions.
(ii) Patterns of inheritance:
• Dominance — in a heterozygous pair of genes, the dominant allele is expressed over the recessive allele, so the F$_1$ progeny resemble the dominant parent.
• Co-dominance — in a pair of genes, both alleles express themselves, so the F$_1$ generation resembles both the parents.
• Incomplete dominance — in the heterozygous state neither allele is able to express itself fully, so the phenotype of the F$_1$ progeny is intermediate between those of the two parents.

questions.text: (b) In a particular cattle, the coat colour red and white are controlled by single pair of alleles. A calf that receives allele for red coat from mother and allele for white coat from father shows equal number of red and white hairs on its coat. (i) Is this an example of Co-dominance or incomplete dominance ? Give a reason for your answer. (ii) With the help of a genetic cross upto F2 generation, explain what will be the consequent phenotype of calf when (1) Red is dominant over white, (2) Red is incompletely dominant.

answer.text:
(i) Co-dominance means two different alleles of a gene are both able to express themselves fully, so both characters appear equally in the heterozygote.

(1) If red is completely dominant over white:
Pure-breeding red $RR$ × pure-breeding white $rr$ gives $F_1$ all $Rr$ (red coat). Selfing the $F_1$ ($Rr \times Rr$) gives the $F_2$ shown below.
$F_2$ phenotypic ratio = 3 Red : 1 White.

(2) If red is incompletely dominant over white:
$RR$ × $rr$ gives $F_1$ all $Rr$ (pink coat — a blend). Selfing the $F_1$ ($Rr \times Rr$) gives the $F_2$ shown below.
$F_2$ phenotypic ratio = 1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White.

questions.text: (b) The following questions are based on haemophilia. (ii) Write the conclusions you draw from these crosses. Comment on the type of inheritance of the disease. (Use : X – Normal, Xh – Haemophilic)

answer.text:
(b) Inheritance of haemophilia (a sex-linked recessive disorder):
(I) A cross between a normal female ($XX$) and a haemophilic male ($X^h Y$) gives all normal offspring — carrier daughters ($XX^h$) and normal sons ($XY$).
(II) A cross between a carrier female ($XX^h$) and a normal male ($XY$) gives normal daughters ($XX$), carrier daughters ($XX^h$), normal sons ($XY$) and haemophilic sons ($X^h Y$) — the Punnett squares are shown below.
(A cross of a carrier female with a haemophilic male can even give a haemophilic daughter.)
(ii) Conclusions: haemophilia is transmitted from an unaffected carrier female to some of the male progeny; the possibility of a female being haemophilic is extremely rare (as her mother must be a carrier and her father haemophilic). It is a sex-linked recessive disorder.

questions.text: (b) In case of any dispute, a very small sample of tissue or even a drop of blood can help us to determine the paternity of a child. Provide a scientific explanation to substantiate the statement.

answer.text: DNA fingerprinting is the basis of paternity testing, because there is a high degree of polymorphism in DNA and these polymorphisms are heritable. Steps: isolation of the DNA and its amplification by PCR; digestion of the DNA; separation of the DNA fragments by electrophoresis; blotting and hybridisation; detection of the hybridised fragments by autoradiography; and matching the DNA bands of the father and the child.

questions.text: (b) (i) Draw a schematic, self-explanatory labelled diagram of lac operon in 'switched on condition'. (ii) Why is regulation of lac operon referred to as negative regulation ?

answer.text:
lac operon in the presence of an inducer: the inducer binds to and inactivates the repressor, so RNA polymerase is able to transcribe the structural genes z, y and a into lac mRNA, which is translated into $\beta$-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.
In the absence of an inducer, the repressor binds to the operator and inhibits gene expression.

questions.text: (b) With reference to the lac operon : (i) Explain the structural genes of lac operon. (ii) Explain how the lac operon is switched on and switched off.

answer.text: Switching 'on' of the lac operon: the lac operon has one regulatory gene (i) and three structural genes (z, y, a). The i gene codes for the repressor; the z gene codes for $\beta$-galactosidase (which hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose); the y gene codes for permease (which increases the cell's permeability to lactose). Normally the repressor protein binds to the operator region and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon. Lactose is the inducer: in its presence, lactose (allolactose) inactivates the repressor by binding to it, which allows RNA polymerase to access the promoter, and transcription proceeds. Because the repressor binds the operator to inhibit gene expression, the lac operon is said to be negatively regulated.

questions.text: (B) Explain with the help of well-labelled diagrams how lac operon operates in E. coli : (i) In presence of an inducer. (ii) In absence of an inducer.

answer.text:
The $lac$ operon (diagrams below):
(i) In the presence of the inducer (lactose): the inducer binds to and inactivates the repressor, so RNA polymerase is able to transcribe the operon. The $lac$ mRNA is translated to give the three enzymes $\beta$-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.
(ii) In the absence of the inducer: the repressor (the product of the $i$ gene) binds to the operator region ($o$) and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.

questions.text: (b) (i) Differentiate between a DNA and RNA nucleotide. (ii) Name the two types of bonds present within a single nucleotide.

answer.text:
(b)(i) Difference between a DNA nucleotide and an RNA nucleotide (any one): a DNA nucleotide has deoxyribose sugar and the nitrogen bases A, G, C, T; an RNA nucleotide has ribose sugar and the nitrogen bases A, G, C, U.
(ii) Bonds in a nucleotide: an N-glycosidic linkage (between the sugar and the base) and a phosphoester linkage (between the sugar and the phosphate).

questions.text: Gene expresses itself in a cell system as a protein/enzyme. How does an expression of gene occur in a cell system and when does it need to occur, and how the gene expression is regulated in a prokaryote cell system was studied by the combined efforts of Jacque Monod, the biochemist and Francois Jacob, the geneticist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli, by which they were able to elucidate the lac operon, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965. answer.text:
(a) In the presence of lactose the repressor protein does not bind to the operator region (O), so RNA polymerase is able to transcribe the operon.
In the absence of lactose the repressor protein binds to the operator region (O) and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.
(b) The permease enzyme, coded by gene 'y', is required to let lactose enter the cell, so that the operon can be switched on.
(c) 'i' stands for the inhibitor (regulatory) gene; it transcribes the repressor protein, which binds to the operator site and switches the operon off.
(d) In the absence of an inducer: the i-gene forms repressor mRNA and then the repressor protein, which binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase, so the structural genes z, y and a are not transcribed.
In the presence of an inducer: the inducer inactivates the repressor; RNA polymerase transcribes z, y and a into lac mRNA, which is translated into $\beta$-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.

questions.text: If the base adenine constitutes 31% of an isolated DNA fragment, then write what will be the expected percentage of the base cytosine in it. Explain how did you arrive at the answer given.

answer.text: By Chargaff's rule, the amount of $A = T$ and $G = C$, and $A + G = C + T$ — i.e. the ratio of adenine to thymine and of guanine to cytosine is constant and equal to one. So if $A = 31\%$, then $T = 31\%$ and $A + T = 62\%$; therefore $C + G = 100 - 62 = 38\%$, giving $C = \dfrac{38}{2} = 19\%$.

questions.text: (a) Why does DNA replication occur within a replication fork and not in its entire length simultaneously ? (b) \"DNA replication is continuous and discontinuous on the two strands within the replication fork.\" Explain with the help of a schematic representation.

answer.text:
(a) Replication is discontinuous on one strand because carrying out replication continuously on both strands would be energetically very expensive (it would require a very high input of energy).
(b) DNA-dependent DNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation along the template strand only in one direction, $5' \rightarrow 3'$. So on the template strand with polarity $3' \rightarrow 5'$ the replication is continuous, while on the other strand (with polarity $5' \rightarrow 3'$) the replication is discontinuous (forming short Okazaki fragments).

questions.text: (a) Write the features a molecule should have to act as a genetic material. In the light of the above features, evaluate and justify the suitability of the molecule that is preferred as an ideal genetic material.

answer.text:
(a) Properties an ideal genetic material should have (any four): it should be able to generate its replica (replication); it should be chemically and structurally stable; it should provide scope for slow changes (mutations) required for evolution; and it should be able to express itself in the form of 'Mendelian characters'.
Why DNA is preferred over RNA as the genetic material (any two): DNA is double-stranded whereas RNA is single-stranded; DNA has thymine instead of the uracil present in RNA, which makes DNA more stable; DNA has a 2'-H group whereas RNA has a reactive 2'-OH group at every nucleotide, which makes RNA easily degradable; and although both can mutate, RNA mutates faster than DNA. Based on these points, the DNA molecule is preferred as the ideal genetic material.

questions.text: (a) (i) Watson and Crick's discovery of double helical structure was based on which two findings. Also mention the name of the scientists associated with these findings. (ii) Write down the salient features of double helix structure of DNA (any three points).

answer.text:
(a)(i) The scientists: Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin — for the X-ray diffraction studies of DNA; and Erwin Chargaff — who showed that in double-stranded DNA the ratios of adenine to thymine and of guanine to cytosine are constant and equal to one.
(ii) Salient features of the double-helix structure of DNA (any three): it is made of two polynucleotide chains, with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases projecting inside; the two chains have antiparallel polarity; the bases of the two strands are paired through hydrogen bonds (adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with thymine, and guanine forms three with cytosine); the two chains are coiled in a right-handed fashion, with a pitch of 3.4 nm and about 10 base pairs per turn (the distance between adjacent base pairs being about 0.34 nm); and the plane of one base pair stacks over the next.

questions.text: (a) (i) Describe the series of experiments conducted by Frederick Griffith. Comment on the significance of the result obtained. (ii) State the contribution of Avery, MacLeod and McCarty.

answer.text:
(a)(i) Griffith's experiment: Griffith worked on $Streptococcus\ pneumoniae$, which had two strains — the S (smooth) strain, with a mucous (polysaccharide) coat, which was virulent, and the R (rough) strain, without a coat, which was non-virulent. When live S bacteria were injected into a mouse, the mouse died; with live R bacteria, it lived; with heat-killed S bacteria, it lived; but with heat-killed S + live R bacteria, the mouse died, and living S bacteria were recovered from it. Griffith concluded that some 'transforming principle', transferred from the heat-killed S strain, had enabled the R strain to synthesise the smooth coat and become virulent — i.e. genetic material had been transferred.
(ii) MacLeod, McCarty and Avery worked to determine the biochemical nature of this 'transforming principle'. They purified the biochemicals (DNA, RNA, protein, etc.) from the heat-killed S cells to see which could transform the live R cells into S cells. They found that DNA alone could bring about the transformation; protein-digesting proteases and RNA-digesting RNases did not affect the transformation, but DNase (which digests DNA) did stop it. Hence they concluded that DNA is the hereditary material.

questions.text: Draw a labelled diagram of a 'replicating fork' showing the polarity. Why does DNA replication occur within such 'fork' ?

answer.text:
The process of DNA replication at the replication fork is shown below: the two strands of the template (parental) DNA separate; on one template continuous synthesis occurs (the leading strand), while on the other template discontinuous synthesis occurs (the lagging strand), the newly synthesised strands growing in the $5'\rightarrow 3'$ direction.
Replication of DNA occurs within a small replication fork (and not by opening up the whole molecule at once) because, DNA being a very long molecule, separation of the two strands along its entire length would require a very high amount of energy.

questions.text: Industrial melanism in England after 1850 is an excellent example of Natural selection. Explain how ?

Industrial melanism (the peppered moth):
Before industrialisation, a thick growth of almost-white lichens covered the tree trunks and walls. From the mixed population of white- and black-winged moths, the white-winged moths survived and increased in number due to camouflage, while the dark-coloured moths were picked out by predators and decreased.
After industrialisation, the tree trunks became dark due to industrial smoke and soot (and the absence of lichens). Now the dark-coloured moths survived and increased due to camouflage, while the white-winged moths were picked out by predators and decreased.

questions.text: (a) How is Hardy-Weinberg expression (p² + 2pq + q²) = 1 derived ? (b) List any two factors that disturb the genetic equilibrium.

answer.text:
(a) According to the Hardy–Weinberg principle, the sum total of all the allelic frequencies in a population is 1. Let there be two alleles, A and a, with frequencies p and q respectively, so that $p + q = 1$. The frequency of the homozygous AA genotype is $p^2$ (the probability that an allele A of frequency p appears on both chromosomes of a diploid individual is $p \times p = p^2$); similarly, the frequency of aa is $q^2$, and that of the heterozygote Aa is $2pq$. Hence $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$.
(b) Factors that disturb the Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (any two): gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, and natural selection.

questions.text: (A) Answer the following questions : (i) State what do you understand by \"MALT\" ? Where is it located inside our body ? (ii) Explain cytokine barriers. answer.text:
(i) MALT is Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue; it is located within the lining of the major tracts — respiratory, digestive and urogenital.
(ii) Cytokine barriers — virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons which protect the non-infected cells from further viral infection.

The bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced, and some lymphocytes migrate to the thymus for their development and maturation.

questions.text: (a) (i) Name the protozoan species that is responsible for causing the most serious and even fatal malarial disease. answer.text:
(a)(i) The parasite is $Plasmodium\ falciparum$.
(ii) The vector is the female $Anopheles$ mosquito. In it: the mosquito picks up the gametocytes from an infected person; fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's gut; and the sporozoites from the gut migrate to the salivary glands of the mosquito.
(iii) After entering the bloodstream, the parasites enter the liver and then the red blood cells and reproduce asexually; the RBCs rupture and release the toxic substance haemozoin, which causes the recurring chills and high fever.
(iv) Preventive measures (any two): avoiding the stagnation of water in and around residential areas; regular cleaning of household coolers; the use of mosquito nets; introducing larvivorous fishes such as $Gambusia$ into ponds; and spraying insecticides and fixing wire mesh on doors and windows.

questions.text: (a) A person inhales dust and pathogens but does not always fall sick. Explain how the body protects against such infections. (b) Name and describe any two barriers involved in this protection.

answer.text:
(a) An 'immune' individual does not fall ill, owing to the immune response of the body — its ability to fight against foreign agents (pathogens).
(b) Innate immune barriers (any two):
• Physical barrier — the skin prevents the entry of pathogens; the mucus coating of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urinogenital tracts helps to trap the microbes entering the body.
• Physiological barrier — the acid in the stomach, the saliva in the mouth and the tears from the eyes all prevent microbial growth.
• Cellular barrier — neutrophils and monocytes in the blood, and macrophages in the tissues, can phagocytose and destroy the microbes.
• Cytokine barrier — virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons that protect the non-infected cells from further viral infection.

questions.text: (a) A 30 year old man was admitted to a hospital with recurrent infections, weight loss, prolonged fever. His blood report showed a decline in count of T-Lymphocytes thus affecting immune system. (i) Identify the disease and its causative agent. (ii) How did the pathogen affect the immune system once it entered the body ? Explain. (iii) Mention two major modes of its transmission.

answer.text:
(a)(i) The disease is Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS); the causative agent is the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) — a retrovirus (replication cycle shown below).
(ii) After gaining entry into the body, the virus enters the macrophages; the RNA genome of the virus replicates to form viral DNA with the help of the enzyme reverse transcriptase; the viral DNA gets incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the infected cell to produce virus particles; simultaneously, HIV enters the helper T-lymphocytes ($T_H$) and produces progeny viruses that attack the other T-lymphocytes, leading to a weakened immune system.
(iii) Modes of transmission of HIV (any two): by sexual contact with an infected person; by the transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products; by the sharing of infected needles among intravenous drug abusers; and from an infected mother to her child through the placenta.

• Bacteria — $Rhizobium$ forms a symbiotic association with the roots of leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms usable by the plant; $Azotobacter$ / $Azospirillum$ fix atmospheric nitrogen while free-living in the soil.
• Fungi — the genus $Glomus$ forms mycorrhiza with plant roots, helping the plant to absorb phosphorus from the soil (and conferring resistance to root pathogens and tolerance to salinity and drought).
• Cyanobacteria — $Anabaena$ / $Nostoc$ / $Oscillatoria$ fix atmospheric nitrogen and serve as important biofertilisers in paddy fields.
(iii) Advantages of biofertilisers over chemical fertilisers (any two): they do not pollute the environment (soil and groundwater); they conserve the beneficial soil microbes; and they do not cause contamination or harm to human health.

questions.text: (b) (i) Why are microbes considered effective biocontrol agents in sustainable agriculture ? (ii) Explain the role of the following as biocontrol agents naming the pests or diseases they help to control : (1) A Bacterium (2) A Fungus (3) Virus.

answer.text:
(b)(i) Advantages of biological control (any): it reduces our dependence on toxic chemicals and pesticides; and it creates a system in which the pest insects are not eradicated but kept at a manageable level by a complex system of checks and balances, with no negative impact on plants, mammals, birds, fishes or non-target insects.
(ii) Examples of biocontrol agents:
(1) A bacterium — $Bacillus\ thuringiensis$ controls butterfly caterpillars; the larvae eat the spores and the toxin is released in the gut of the larvae, killing them.
(2) A fungus — $Trichoderma$, a free-living fungus common in the root ecosystem, is an effective biocontrol agent against several plant pathogens.
(3) A virus — the baculoviruses (genus $Nucleopolyhedrovirus$) show a species-specific, narrow-spectrum insecticidal application.

questions.text: Treatment of wastewater is done in a sewage treatment plant to make it less polluting. Explain the following with reference to this treatment process : (a) Primary sludge (b) Activated sludge (c) Anaerobic sludge digesters

answer.text:
(a) Primary sludge: all the solids that settle down during the primary treatment of sewage water.
(b) Activated sludge: the sediment produced during the secondary (biological) treatment — the primary effluent together with aerobic microbial flocs (bacteria and fungi), whose BOD has been reduced significantly.
(c) Anaerobic sludge digesters: large tanks in which the activated sludge is digested by anaerobic bacteria, producing a mixture of $CH_4$, $H_2S$ and $CO_2$ (biogas).

questions.text: After significant reduction of BOD during secondary treatment of sewage, what further processes are carried out ? Mention any one important outcome of these processes.

answer.text:
Later steps of sewage treatment:
• The effluent from the aeration tank is passed into settling tanks, where the flocs settle down to form the activated sludge.
• A small part of the activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank to serve as inoculum, while the major remaining part is pumped into large tanks called anaerobic sludge digesters.
• The anaerobic bacteria digest the sludge and produce a mixture of gases — methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide — i.e. biogas.
The biogas produced can be used as a source of energy; the effluent from the secondary treatment plant is generally released into natural water bodies such as rivers and streams.

questions.text: With the help of a schematic diagram only, show in three steps, the formation of recombinant DNA by the action of restriction endonuclease — EcoRI and DNA ligase.

answer.text:
Formation of recombinant DNA using the restriction enzyme EcoRI:
• EcoRI cuts both the vector DNA and the foreign DNA at the same palindromic recognition sequence, $5'$-GAATTC-$3'$, between G and A on each strand.
• This staggered cut leaves complementary single-stranded 'sticky ends' (AATT overhangs) on both DNA molecules.
• The sticky end of the foreign DNA base-pairs with the complementary sticky end of the vector DNA.
• DNA ligase then seals the joins to produce the recombinant DNA molecule.

questions.text: Answer the following questions with respect to recombinant DNA technology : (i) Why is plasmid considered to be an important tool in rDNA technology ? answer.text:
(i) A good cloning vector can act as a vector / self-replicate to form multiple copies / carry selectable markers / be small in size (to facilitate insertion) / possess an origin of replication ('Ori'). Examples: E. coli, $Agrobacterium\ tumefaciens$, $Salmonella\ typhi$, bacteria (any two).
(ii) 'Ori' — the sequence from where replication starts; any piece of DNA linked to it can be replicated within the host cell, and it controls the copy number of the linked DNA. A selectable marker helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants, selectively permitting the growth of transformants.
(iii) A restriction endonuclease recognises a specific palindromic sequence and cuts the DNA at specific sites in both the host and the foreign DNA, creating 'sticky ends' that facilitate ligation to form recombinant DNA.

questions.text: (a) (i) Explain any two basic principles/core techniques on which biotechnology is based. (ii) Describe any three key tools used in Recombinant DNA technology.

• Micro-injection — recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell.
• Biolistics / gene gun — plant cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA.
• Heat shock — recombinant DNA is forced into cells by incubating them with the DNA on ice, briefly placing them at 42 °C (heat shock), and then putting them back on ice.

questions.text: (b) Explain the amplification of gene of interest using the technique of Polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

answer.text:
(b) Each cycle of PCR (diagram below) has three steps:
• Denaturation — the DNA is subjected to a higher temperature and the two strands separate as the hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous bases are broken.
• Annealing — two sets of primers, which are complementary to the 3' ends of the two template strands, attach to them.
• Extension — a new strand of DNA is formed using the thermostable Taq polymerase (derived from the bacterium $Thermus\ aquaticus$), which extends the primers using the nucleotides provided and the genomic DNA as the template.
When this cycle of replication is repeated about 30 times, the segment of DNA is amplified about a billion times.

questions.text: (b) Describe the structure and working of a sparged stirred-tank bioreactor.

answer.text: A stirred-tank bioreactor (diagram below) is a large vessel/container that provides the optimal conditions to produce the desired product. It contains a stirrer, which facilitates even mixing and oxygen availability throughout the bioreactor. Air is bubbled through the reactor to increase the oxygen-transfer area. It also has a foam-control system, a temperature-control system, a pH-control system, salts, vitamins, and sampling ports, so that small volumes of the culture can be withdrawn periodically.

questions.text: (b) (i) Explain how the amplification of gene of interest is done using PCR. (ii) State two applications of the desired amplified fragment of DNA.

answer.text:
(i) The three steps of PCR (diagram below):
• Denaturation — the two strands of DNA are separated at a high temperature.
• Annealing of the primer — two sets of primers bind to the single-stranded template DNA.
• Extension — the enzyme Taq polymerase extends the primers using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as the template.
(ii) The amplified fragments can be used (any two): to ligate with a vector for further cloning, in DNA fingerprinting, for recombinant-protein synthesis, and in the diagnosis of diseases.

questions.text: (b) In order to force bacteria to take up the recombinant DNA, they must be made competent. Explain how it can be achieved.

answer.text:
(b) Making bacterial cells competent to take up recombinant DNA:
– Treat the bacterial cells with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as $Ca^{2+}$.
– Incubate the bacteria (host) with the recombinant DNA on ice.
– Place them at $42\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ (give a brief heat shock at $42\,^{\circ}\text{C}$).
– Put them back on ice; this enables the bacteria to take up the recombinant DNA.

questions.text: Explain how recombinant DNA technology is used to detect a disease even before any clinical symptom appears.

answer.text:
A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule (a probe) is allowed to hybridise with its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, followed by detection using autoradiography; the clone carrying the mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film.
(Alternatively, PCR is used to detect a disease even before any clinical symptoms appear — it involves denaturation and annealing to amplify the pathogen's DNA using pathogen-specific primers.)

questions.text: Answer the following questions based on Bt-crops : (i) Why do farmers prefer to grow Bt cotton crop than genetically unmodified cotton crops ? (ii) Name any two insects that are killed by Bt toxin. (iii) Explain the mechanism by which Bt toxin kills the insects but not the bacterium which possesses the toxin.

answer.text:
(i) Bt cotton is pest-resistant / insect-resistant and gives increased productivity.
(ii) Cotton bollworms / corn borer / tobacco budworm / army worm / coleopterans (beetles) / dipterans (flies, mosquitoes) (any two).
(iii) The Bt toxin exists as an inactive protoxin in the bacterium. Once ingested by the insect it is converted to the active form, because the alkaline pH of the gut solubilises the inactive crystals. The activated toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, causing cell swelling and lysis and, eventually, the death of the insect.

questions.text: (b) 'Bt cotton', the genetically modified crop, has greatly helped the cotton farmers to increase their crop yield. (i) How was Bt cotton plant made resistant to bollworm ? Explain. (ii) Describe the mechanism that leads to the death of bollworms feeding on Bt cotton plants.

answer.text:
(i) The specific Bt toxin gene (cryIAc / cryIIAb), isolated from $Bacillus\ thuringiensis$, is incorporated into the cotton plant to give it resistance to the bollworm.
(ii) $Bacillus\ thuringiensis$ forms a toxic insecticidal protein (the Bt toxin) during a particular growth phase. The Bt toxin exists as an inactive protoxin; on ingestion by the bollworm, it is converted to the active form due to the alkaline pH of the gut. The activated toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells, creates pores, and causes cell swelling, lysis and the death of the insect.

questions.text: (b) (i) Name the nematode (scientific name) that infects the roots of tobacco plant and reduces its yield. (ii) Name the vector that is used to introduce nematode-specific genes into the host plant (tobacco). (iii) How do sense and anti-sense RNAs function ? (iv) Why could parasite not survive in a transgenic tobacco plant ?

answer.text:
(i) $Meloidogyne\ incognita$.
(ii) $Agrobacterium\ tumefaciens$ / the Ti plasmid.
(iii) The sense and antisense RNA are complementary to each other and pair to form a double-stranded RNA (dsRNA).
(iv) The dsRNA binds to a specific mRNA and initiates RNA interference (RNAi), preventing the translation of / silencing the specific mRNA of the parasite (nematode).

questions.text: (B) (i) What are transgenic animals ? (ii) Why are these animals being produced ? Explain any four reasons.

answer.text:
(i) Transgenic animals — animals that have had their DNA manipulated so as to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are known as transgenic animals.
(ii) Common reasons for producing transgenic animals (any four):
• Normal physiology and development — to study how genes are regulated and how they affect the normal functions of the body and its development.
• Study of disease — many are made to serve as models for human diseases so that new treatments can be investigated.
• Biological products — transgenic animals can be created to produce useful biological products.
• Vaccine safety — transgenic mice are developed for testing the safety of vaccines before they are used on humans.
• Chemical safety testing — transgenic animals are made carrying genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals.

questions.text: (b) \"Early and accurate diagnosis of diseases is vital in medical technology.\" (i) Name the conventional methods of diagnosis and their disadvantages. (ii) Which three diagnostic techniques have been developed through Biotechnology ? Explain how each one helps in detecting diseases.

answer.text:
(b)(i) A conventional diagnostic method (any one): urine analysis / stool analysis / sputum analysis / serum analysis. Disadvantage: early detection is not possible — the disease is detected only after it has spread or shows symptoms.
(ii) Three molecular diagnostic techniques:
• PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) — it amplifies specific DNA sequences from very small samples, allowing very early detection.
• ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay) — based on the antigen–antibody interaction; an infection can be detected by the presence of the antigen, or by detecting the antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.
• Molecular (DNA/RNA) probe — a single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule is created; it binds to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells and is then detected by autoradiography (a clone with a mutated gene will not appear on the film, as it lacks complementarity).

questions.text: (a) How is insulin different from proinsulin ? (b) Explain all the stages of how human insulin is produced through rDNA technology.

answer.text:
(a) Proinsulin contains an extra stretch called the C-peptide, in addition to the A and B chains; this C-peptide is not present in the mature insulin.
(b) Steps to produce insulin by rDNA technology:
– Eli Lilly (an American company) prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin.
– These A and B chains were then introduced into plasmids of $E.\ coli$ to produce multiple copies.
– The chains A and B were then extracted separately.
– Chains A and B were combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin.

questions.text: Transgenic animals are produced by man. Explain any three ways in which such animals can be beneficial to humans.

answer.text:
Uses of transgenic animals (any three, with explanation):
– Normal physiology and development: to study how genes are regulated and how they affect normal body functions and development (e.g. the role of complex factors such as insulin-like growth factor).
– Study of disease: to study how genes contribute to the development of a disease; such model animals help us study diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's, and to investigate new treatments.
– Biological products: to produce useful biological products / medicines (e.g. the human protein $\alpha$-1-antitrypsin used to treat emphysema; treatment of phenylketonuria and cystic fibrosis; the transgenic cow Rosie produced human-protein-enriched milk).
– Vaccine safety: transgenic mice are used to test the safety of vaccines (e.g. the polio vaccine) before they are used on humans, and could replace the use of monkeys.
– Chemical safety testing: transgenic animals made more sensitive to toxic substances are exposed to those substances and the effects are studied.

questions.text: Explain the following population interactions with the help of one example each : (a) Brood Parasitism (b) Co-evolution of mutualists

answer.text:
(a) Brood parasitism: a parasitic bird lays eggs resembling the host bird's eggs in the host's nest. For example, the cuckoo (koel) lays its eggs in the crow's nest; the koel's eggs have evolved to resemble the crow's eggs, and the koel lets the crow hatch them.
(b) Co-evolution: when the evolution of one species is tightly linked with the evolution of another species; e.g. plant–pollinator interaction, or the fig species and its specific wasp.

questions.text: Predation is referred to as a detrimental interaction. Explain any three positive roles, supported by an example each, that a predator plays in an ecosystem.

answer.text:
Roles of predators in an ecosystem (any two, with an example):
• They act as conduits for energy transfer across trophic levels — e.g. grass → goat → lion, where the lion transfers the energy fixed by plants through the ecosystem.
• They keep prey populations under control — e.g. the cactus-feeding moth controls the spread of the prickly-pear cactus.
• They help maintain species diversity by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species — e.g. the removal of the starfish $Pisaster$ (a predator) led to the extinction of more than 10 species of invertebrates.

questions.text: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness in the habitat in which they live. Ecologists suggest, the life history of organisms have evolved in relations to the constraints imposed by the biotic and abiotic components of the habitat in which they live. This gets reflected in the population growth pattern of all organisms including humans. Study the population growth curves shown in the given graph and answer the questions that follow : (a) Identify the growth curves 'A' and 'B'. (b) Mention what does the dotted line in the graph indicate and state its importance also. OR (b) Growth curve 'B' shows a different pattern from that of growth curve 'A'. Justify giving one reason. (c) (i) Which one of the two curves is more \"realistic\" and why ? (ii) Which one of the two curves is relevant in present days with respect to human population in our country and why ?

answer.text:
(a) A — the exponential (J-shaped) growth curve; B — the logistic (S-shaped / sigmoid) growth curve.
(b) It represents the carrying capacity (K) — the maximum possible number of individuals beyond which no further growth of the population is observed. (Curve B forms when the resources (food and space) in nature are limited, with environmental checks, while curve A forms when the resources are unlimited with no environmental checks.)
(c)(i) Curve B (the logistic growth curve), because resources are never infinite in nature.
(ii) The J-shaped curve (exponential growth) — a continuously growing population.

questions.text: Observe the population growth curve and answer the questions given below : (a) State the conditions under which growth curve 'A' and growth curve 'B' plotted in the graph are possible. (b) Mention what does 'K' in the graph represent.

answer.text:
(a) Growth curve A — formed when there are unlimited resources (food and space), no competition, and no environmental checks/resistance. Growth curve B — formed when the resources are limited, there is more competition, and environmental checks/resistance are present.
(b) 'K' is the carrying capacity — the maximum number of individuals of a population that a given habitat can accommodate (beyond which no further growth is possible).

questions.text: In nature, we rarely find isolated, single individuals of any species; majority of them live in groups in a well-defined geographical area, share or compete for similar resources, potentially interbreed and thus constitute a population. The population has certain attributes whereas, an individual organism does not. A population at a given time is composed of individuals of different ages. The size of the population tells us a lot about its status in the habitat. Population density (N) need not necessarily be measured in numbers only. (a) The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator because of a special chemical present in its body. How does the butterfly acquire this chemical ? (b) If population density at a time t + 1 was 800, Emigration = 100, Immigration = 200, Natality = 200 and Mortality = 150, calculate the population density at time t and comment upon the type of age pyramid that will be formed in this case. (c) What is the difference in a method of measuring population density if there are 200 carrot grass plants to only single huge banyan tree ? OR (d) Name two methods to measure the population density of tigers.

answer.text:
(a) The butterfly acquires this chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed.
(b) Using $N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]$:
$800 = N_t + [(200 + 200) - (150 + 100)] = N_t + (400 - 250) = N_t + 150$, so $N_t = 800 - 150 = 650$.
Comment: as the population density is increasing with time, the age pyramid would be that of an expanding population.
(c) A single huge banyan tree — measured in terms of biomass or percent cover; carrot grass — measured in terms of percent cover.
OR (d) The tiger is counted using indirect signs such as pug marks and faecal pellets.

questions.text: (a) Draw a graph for a population whose population density has reached the carrying capacity. (b) Out of the two population growth curves, which one is considered a more realistic for most populations ? Why ? (c) Draw a growth curve where resources are not limiting for the growth of a population and give its equation.

answer.text:
(a) The graph is a sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve rising to the carrying capacity (K).
(b) It is the Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth curve (sigmoid growth curve). A population grows this way because the resources for growth of most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later.
(c) The other type is the exponential (geometric) growth curve (J-shaped), which occurs when resources are unlimited. Its equation is $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN$ (i.e. $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = (b-d)N$), giving $N_t = N_0 e^{rt}$.

questions.text: (a) Explain how the interaction between sea anemone and clownfish is one of the best examples of commensalism in nature.

answer.text: (a) The clownfish gets protection from predators due to the presence of the stinging tentacles of the sea anemone, thus deriving benefit from it, while the sea anemone neither derives any benefit nor is harmed by the clownfish. (This is commensalism.)

questions.text: (a) (i) Describe the population growth curve applicable in a population of any species in nature that has limited resources at its disposal. (ii) Give the equation of this growth curve. (iii) Name the growth curve and depict a graphical plot for this type of population growth.

answer.text:
(i) A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows a characteristic sigmoid (logistic) growth: an initial lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when the population density reaches the carrying capacity (K).
(ii) The logistic growth equation is $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\dfrac{K-N}{K}\right)$, where N = population density at time t, r = the intrinsic rate of natural increase, and K = the carrying capacity.
(iii) This is the logistic growth curve (Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth / sigmoid / S-shaped curve); its plot is shown below.

questions.text: (a) Explain how the interaction between a fig tree and its tight one-to-one relationship with the pollinator species of wasp is one of the best examples of mutualism.

answer.text: (a) A fig species can be pollinated only by its 'partner' wasp species and no other species. The female wasp uses the fruit not only as an oviposition (egg-laying) site but also uses the developing seeds within the fruit for nourishing its larvae; while searching for a suitable egg-laying site, the wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence. (This is an example of mutualism / a one-to-one plant–pollinator relationship.)

questions.text: (a) (i) Describe the population growth curve applicable in a population of any species in nature that has unlimited resources at its disposal. (ii) Explain the equation of this growth curve. (iii) Name the growth curve and depict a graphical plot for this type of population growth.

answer.text:
(i) When the resources in the habitat are unlimited, each species has the ability to realise fully its innate potential to grow in number; the population then grows in an exponential (geometric) fashion, giving a J-shaped curve when the population density is plotted against time.
(ii) The equation is $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = (b-d)N = rN$, giving $N_t = N_0 e^{rt}$, where r = the intrinsic rate of natural increase, N = the size of the population, b = birth rate and d = death rate.
(iii) This is the exponential (J-shaped) growth curve, shown below.

questions.text: A biologist studied the population of rats in a granary. He found the average natality was 280, average mortality was 200, immigration was 40 and emigration was 50. The net increase in population is :

The diagram below shows the distribution of two barnacle species, Chthamalus and Balanus on a rocky sea shore. When Balanus is experimentally removed, Chthamalus expands its range in lower intertidal zone. (a) Identify and define the ecological phenomenon demonstrated by this observation. OR (a) State the principle that explains the elimination of one species. (b) Two different species can compete for the same resource. Give another example of it. (c) How do species avoid competition in nature ? Explain with an example.

answer.text:
(a) Competitive release. It is the phenomenon in which a species whose distribution is restricted to a small geographical area (because of the presence of a competitively superior species) expands its distributional range when the competing superior species is removed.
OR (a) Gause's competitive exclusion principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually.
(b) Example: in the shallow South American lakes, the visiting flamingos and the resident fishes compete for their common food, zooplankton.
(c) By 'resource partitioning' — the competing species choose different times for feeding or different foraging patterns. E.g. five closely related species of warblers avoid competition and co-exist owing to behavioural differences in their foraging activities.

questions.text: (a) In some cases, measuring population density by counting individuals may not be feasible. Mention two other parameters that can be used and justify their use with suitable examples.

answer.text:
Measures of population density (any two):
• Percent cover / biomass — e.g. in an area with 200 carrot-grass ($Parthenium$) plants but a single huge banyan tree with a large canopy, stating that the population density of the banyan is low would grossly underestimate its enormous role, so biomass or percent cover is a more meaningful measure.
• Relative density — e.g. a laboratory culture in a petri dish, or the number of fish caught per trap.
• Indirect estimate — e.g. the tiger census in national parks and reserves, which is often based on pug marks and faecal pellets.

questions.text: (a) What is the carrying capacity of a species in a habitat ? (b) Explain the growth curve that takes this capacity into account.

answer.text:
(a) Carrying capacity (K) denotes the limit — the maximum number of individuals of a species (population) that a given habitat can support with its available resources.
(b) The growth curve is called the Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth curve. A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows an initial lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when the population density reaches the carrying capacity — giving a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve (below). It is described by $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\dfrac{K-N}{K}\right)$, where N = the population at time t, r = the intrinsic rate of natural increase, and K = the carrying capacity.

questions.text: (b) Answer the following questions : (i) Define 'predation'. (ii) Why is predation required in a community of different organisms ? Give any two points. (iii) Why are predators 'prudent' in nature ?

answer.text:
(b)(i) Predation is the interspecific interaction in which a larger animal, called the predator, kills and consumes a smaller animal, called the prey.
(ii) Roles of predators (any two):
– They keep the prey population under control.
– They help in maintaining species diversity in a community by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.
– They act as a conduit for energy transfer across trophic levels.
– Biological control methods used in agricultural pest control are based on the ability of a predator to regulate the prey population.
(iii) If a predator is too efficient and over-exploits its prey, the prey may become extinct and, following that, the predator will also become extinct for lack of food.
