questions.text: Explain Gause's 'Competitive Exclusion Principle' with the help of a suitable example.

answer.text:
– Gause's competitive exclusion principle states that two closely related species competing for the same limited resources cannot co-exist indefinitely, and the competitively inferior one will eventually be eliminated (if resources are limited, the stronger competitor dominates and drives the weaker one to extinction).
– Example: in some shallow American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, i.e. zooplankton; or, the Abingdon tortoise in the Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, probably because of the greater browsing efficiency of the goats.

questions.text: (b) Explain Brood parasitism with the help of a suitable example.

answer.text: Brood parasitism is a method of parasitism in which the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of the host bird and lets the host incubate them. Example: the cuckoo lays its eggs in the crow's nest; the cuckoo's eggs resemble the crow's eggs in size and colour, reducing the chance of the host detecting and ejecting them.

questions.text: (b) (i) Describe the logistic population growth curve with the help of a suitable graphical representation. (ii) Write the equation of Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth curve and explain what 'K' and 'r' suggest in the given equation.

answer.text:
(i) A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows a characteristic logistic growth (graph below): an initial lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration, and finally an asymptote when the population density reaches the carrying capacity (K).
(ii) The logistic growth is described by $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\dfrac{K-N}{K}\right)$, where N = the population density at time t, r = the intrinsic rate of natural increase, and K = the carrying capacity (the maximum possible number in a given habitat).

questions.text: (b) (i) Write an equation for Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth Curve where N = Population density at time t, r = Intrinsic rate of natural increase. (ii) Draw a graph for a population whose population density has reached carrying capacity. (iii) Draw a growth curve where resources are non-limiting to growth of population. (iv) Which growth curve is considered more realistic and why ? Explain.

answer.text:
(b)(i) The logistic (Verhulst–Pearl) growth is described by $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\dfrac{K-N}{K}\right)$.
(ii) When resources are limited, the growth is sigmoid (S-shaped), levelling off at the carrying capacity — the sigmoid growth curve (first graph below).
(iii) When resources are unlimited, the growth is exponential, giving a J-shaped growth curve (second graph below).
(iv) The logistic (sigmoid) growth curve is more realistic, because a given habitat in nature has only enough resources to support a maximum possible number (the carrying capacity), beyond which further growth is not possible as the resources become limiting.

questions.text: (b) Arrange the given important steps of decomposition in their correct order of occurrence in the breakdown of complex organic matter and explain the fourth step in the process : Catabolism, Leaching, Fragmentation, Mineralisation, Humification.

answer.text:
The correct sequence of steps in decomposition is: fragmentation $\rightarrow$ leaching $\rightarrow$ catabolism $\rightarrow$ humification $\rightarrow$ mineralisation.
Humification leads to the accumulation of a dark-coloured amorphous substance called humus, which is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate.

questions.text: (b) Correctly depict (also indicate the trophic level) and describe the ecological pyramid of biomass in sea with 40 standing crop of phytoplankton supporting 90 standing crop of zooplankton which further supports 120 small fishes.

answer.text: (b) An inverted pyramid of biomass — as in a sea / aquatic ecosystem, the biomass of the primary producers (phytoplankton, e.g. 40 units) is the smallest, that of the primary consumers (zooplankton, e.g. 90 units) is larger, and that of the secondary consumers (fishes, e.g. 120 units) is the largest, so the pyramid of biomass is inverted.

questions.text: (b) Correctly depict (also indicate the trophic level) and describe the ecological pyramid of number with 32 birds dependent on 20 insects feeding on one banyan tree.

answer.text: (b) An inverted ecological pyramid of numbers — as in a single big tree (e.g. a banyan tree) supporting an ecosystem: the primary producer (1 tree) is fewest in number, the primary consumers (e.g. 20 insects) are more numerous, and the secondary consumers (e.g. 32 birds) are the most numerous, so the pyramid of numbers is inverted.

questions.text: Ecological pyramids give important information about the ecological system, but do have some limitations. List any two limitations of ecological pyramids.

answer.text:
Limitations of the pyramid of numbers (any two):
• It does not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels.
• It assumes a simple food chain, which never exists in nature; it does not accommodate a food web.
• Saprophytes are not given any place, even though they play an important ecological role.

questions.text: Given below is a food web that involves nine organisms. (a) Identify two producers and two carnivores shown in the food web. (b) Is it possible to make an ecological pyramid depicting this food web ? Give reason in support of your answer.

(b) No — a pyramid of numbers does not accommodate a food web.

questions.text: (a) Analyse the following ecosystems and discuss, which will be more productive in terms of primary productivity : A young forest, a natural old forest, a shallow polluted lake.

A shallow polluted lake contains fewer producers and a high amount of dead organic matter, so its productivity is less than that of the natural old forest.

questions.text: (b) (i) What does an ecological pyramid represent ? (ii) The Ecological pyramids may have an 'upright' or an 'inverted' shape. Justify with the help of suitable examples.

answer.text:
(i) An ecological pyramid is the diagrammatic representation of the relationship between the organisms at different trophic levels (in terms of energy, biomass or the number of organisms in an ecosystem).
(ii) A pyramid is upright when the number / biomass / energy is greater in the producers than in the consumers (e.g. the pyramid in a grassland ecosystem). It is inverted when the number / biomass is less in the producers than in the consumers (e.g. in terms of biomass, a small standing crop of phytoplankton supports a large standing crop of zooplankton, or a single big tree supports a large number of insects).

questions.text: (b) (i) State, what does 'standing crop' of a trophic level represent. (ii) List any two ways of measuring the standing crop of a trophic level.

(ii) It is measured as the biomass (mass of living organisms, i.e. dry weight) per unit area, or as the number per unit area.

questions.text: The world is facing accelerated rates of species extinction largely due to human activities. Explain any three human activities responsible for accelerated rates of species extinction.

answer.text:
Human activities responsible for the loss of biodiversity (any three, with an explanation):
• Habitat loss and fragmentation — e.g. the cutting and clearing of the Amazon rainforest for cultivable land fragments habitats and affects the organisms living there.
• Over-exploitation of natural resources — e.g. Steller's sea cow, the passenger pigeon and many marine fish.
• Alien species invasion — e.g. the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria led to the extinction of 200 species of Cichlid fish; the African catfish ($Clarias\ gariepinus$) threatens indigenous catfish; and $Parthenium$, $Lantana$ and water hyacinth ($Eichhornia$) cause the decline of indigenous species.
• Co-extinction — the extinction of one species (e.g. a partner in a plant–pollinator mutualism) leads to the extinction of its obligatory associate.

questions.text: (a) Indiscriminate human activities such as alien species invasion, fragmentation and habitat loss have accelerated the loss of biodiversity. Justify by taking one example for each. (b) State the importance of the following : (i) IUCN Red data list (ii) Hot spots in conservation of biodiversity

answer.text:
(a) Two ways in which biodiversity is lost:
• Alien species invasion — e.g. the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria (East Africa) led to the extinction of over 200 species of cichlid fish; invasive weeds such as carrot grass ($Parthenium$), $Lantana$ and water hyacinth ($Eichhornia$); the illegal introduction of the African catfish $Clarias\ gariepinus$ threatens the indigenous catfish.
• Habitat loss and fragmentation — when large habitats are broken up into small fragments by human activities, mammals and birds requiring large territories are badly affected, leading to population decline (e.g. the Amazon rainforest being cut and cleared for soya-bean cultivation or cattle raising).
(b)(i) IUCN Red Data List — provides information about species under the threat of extinction / identifies and protects species facing a high risk of extinction; crucial for conservation planning.
(ii) Hotspots — regions with very high levels of species richness and a high degree of endemism.

questions.text: (A) (i) Explain giving three reasons why tropics show greatest levels of species diversity. (ii) Draw a graph showing species-area relationship. Name the naturalist who studied such relationship. Write the observation made by him.

answer.text:
(i) Reasons for the greater biodiversity of tropical latitudes (any):
• Tropical latitudes have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years and thus have had a long evolutionary time for species diversification.
• Tropical environments are less seasonal, more constant and predictable; such constant environments promote niche specialisation and lead to greater species diversity.
• More solar energy is available in the tropics, which contributes to higher productivity and, in turn, to greater species diversity.
(ii) The species–area relationship (graph below): within a region, species richness increases with the explored area, but only up to a limit. This relationship was described by Alexander von Humboldt.

questions.text: (B) (i) The world is facing the accelerated rate of species extinctions due to human activities. Explain any three major causes of biodiversity losses. (ii) Describe 'Ex situ' approach for conserving biodiversity. Give any two examples.

answer.text:
(i) Causes of biodiversity loss (any three):
• Habitat loss and fragmentation — deforestation causes habitat loss and the extinction of animals and plants; when large habitats are broken into small fragments, mammals and birds with large territories and animals with migratory habits are badly affected.
• Over-exploitation — over-exploitation of natural resources by humans leads to the extinction of many species (e.g. Steller's sea cow, the passenger pigeon).
• Alien species invasions — introduced species may turn invasive and cause the decline or extinction of indigenous species (e.g. $Parthenium$, $Lantana$, water hyacinth).
• Co-extinctions — when a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct (e.g. a parasite with its host; a plant with its obligate pollinator).
(ii) Ex-situ conservation — threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and placed in a special setting where they can be protected and given special care (e.g. zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, seed banks, pollen banks).

questions.text: The biggest threat to the tiger's survival in Mudumalai Tiger Reserve (MTR) was found to be a small, beautiful flower, Lantana camara, a tropical American shrub, that invaded 40% of India's tiger range. Tamil Nadu department's Lantana weed eradication drive helped to restore the dying MTR thereby also reducing human-wildlife conflicts. MTR is home to 25 species of grasses and legumes. Answer the given questions based on the information given above. (a) Explain how did the removal of Lantana help in restoring the dying Mudumalai Tiger Reserve. (b) Why is the invasion of Lantana camara a cause of concern in MTR ?

answer.text:
(a) The removal of $Lantana$ allows other plants to grow; because of this, the herbivore population increases, and that in turn helps to restore the tiger population.
(b) $Lantana$, being invasive, does not allow other plants to grow in its surroundings; this leads to a decrease in the herbivore population, which can in turn cause a decline in the tiger population.

questions.text: Enlist one advantage and two disadvantages of green revolution.

answer.text:
Advantage of the Green Revolution (any one): it increased the production of crops and could thus support a larger population in terms of food.
Disadvantages of the Green Revolution (any two): the use of agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides) led to the pollution of the soil and water in the long run (biomagnification); crop-management practices such as irrigation were expensive; the agrochemicals themselves were too expensive; it led to an increase in soil salinity; the agrochemicals reduced the natural soil fertility; and the crops became dependent on fertilisers and pesticides.

questions.text: Explain how the loss of habitat and fragmentation drives plants and animals to extinction with the help of an example of habitat loss in the Tropical Rain Forest. Also write the effect of fragmentation of a habitat on the population decline.

answer.text:
Two causes of biodiversity loss:
• Habitat loss (deforestation) — e.g. the Amazon rainforest is being cut and cleared for cultivating soya beans or for converting grasslands to raise beef cattle, which threatens the survival of many species.
• Habitat fragmentation — when large habitats are broken up into small fragments, mammals and birds requiring large territories, and certain animals with migratory habits, are badly affected, leading to their extinction or population decline.

(b) The two criteria that make a region a biodiversity hotspot: a high degree of endemism, and high levels of species richness.

questions.text: (a) Biodiversity must be conserved as it plays an important role in many ecosystem services that nature provides. Explain any two ecosystem services.

answer.text:
Ecosystem services (any two):
– The Amazon forest produces about 20% of the total oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere.
– Pollination, without which plants cannot give us fruits and seeds, is provided through honeybees, bumblebees, birds and bats.
– Provides aesthetic, cultural and spiritual values.
– Provides wildlife habitat and helps in their sustenance.
– Maintains balance in the various components of the ecosystem through photosynthesis, cycling of nutrients, generating fertile soil, mitigating droughts and controlling floods.
– Provides products of economic importance.

questions.text: There are many animals, which have become extinct in the wild, but continue to be maintained in zoological parks. Answer the questions that follow : (a) What type of bio-diversity conservation is observed in this case ? (b) Explain any other two ways which help in this type of conservation. (c) Besides zoological parks, mention one place that serves this purpose.

answer.text:
(a) Ex-situ conservation.
(b) Methods (any two):
– Cryopreservation: at $-196\,^{\circ}\text{C}$, gametes (sperms or eggs), animal tissues, or embryos of threatened species can be stored.
– In vitro: using tissue-culture methods, plants can be propagated.
– Seed banks: seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be stored.
– Botanical gardens: threatened plants can be conserved in special settings.
(c) Botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks (any one).

questions.text: Which of the following fish led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in Lake Victoria of East Africa ?

answer.text: Nile Perch

questions.text: Explain the level of biodiversity at genetic, species and ecological levels with the help of one example each.

answer.text:
– Genetic diversity: the diversity shown by a single species at the genetic level over its distributional range, e.g. India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice; the medicinal plant $Rauwolfia\ vomitoria$ growing in different Himalayan ranges varies in the potency and concentration of the active chemical (reserpine) it produces.
– Species diversity: the diversity at the species level, i.e. the number of different species in a given region, e.g. the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.
– Ecological diversity: the diversity at the ecosystem level, i.e. the presence of different types of ecosystems in a particular area, e.g. India, with its rain forests, coral reefs, deserts, etc., has a great ecosystem diversity.
